title: Claude Certified Architect — Foundations Concept Graph
description: A pedagogical graph of the mechanisms and decision rules represented by the local CCA-F practice bank. Domain membership is hierarchical; all other edges express learning relationships rather than claims about the live exam.

relationshipTypes.contains: A domain contains a concept in the local learning taxonomy.
relationshipTypes.prerequisite_for: Understanding the source materially helps a learner understand the target.
relationshipTypes.enables: The source is a mechanism or capability used to implement the target.
relationshipTypes.constrains: The source sets a boundary or invariant on the target.
relationshipTypes.mitigates: The source reduces a failure mode represented by the target.
relationshipTypes.complements: The concepts address different parts of the same design problem.
relationshipTypes.contrasts_with: The concepts are commonly confused but require different decisions.
relationshipTypes.produces_evidence_for: The source produces observations used by the target.
relationshipTypes.preserves: The source carries an important property into or across the target.

weightMeaning: Relationship strength from 0.0 to 1.0. It represents pedagogical relevance, not exam probability or empirical causality.

nodes.label: Agentic Architecture & Orchestration
nodes.summary: Design agent loops, delegation, coordination, recovery, and human control points.

nodes.label: Tool Design & MCP Integration
nodes.summary: Design usable tool contracts and integrate MCP capabilities with explicit trust and error boundaries.

nodes.label: Claude Code Configuration & Workflows
nodes.summary: Configure Claude Code, reusable guidance, permissions, and verifiable development workflows.

nodes.label: Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
nodes.summary: Specify tasks, shape reliable outputs, validate meaning, and evaluate quality.

nodes.label: Context Management & Reliability
nodes.summary: Preserve relevant state and provenance while controlling context cost and degradation.

nodes.label: Agentic loop
nodes.summary: Repeatedly let the model decide, execute requested tools, return results, and continue until the protocol marks the turn complete.

nodes.label: Protocol-driven termination
nodes.summary: Use stop_reason and explicit failure states rather than prose inspection or a silent iteration cap to decide completion.

nodes.label: Coordinator decomposition and coverage
nodes.summary: Enumerate dimensions, delegate bounded work, evaluate coverage, and re-delegate gaps.

nodes.label: Subagent isolation and handoffs
nodes.summary: Treat each subagent as a fresh context and pass all required inputs and output contracts explicitly.

nodes.label: Orchestration topology and parallelism
nodes.summary: Choose hub-and-spoke, sequential, or parallel execution from dependency structure and coordination requirements.

nodes.label: Dynamic versus fixed workflows
nodes.summary: Use model-driven routing when later actions depend on newly observed results; fix sequences only when knowable in advance.

nodes.label: Human checkpoints and recovery
nodes.summary: Escalate ambiguous, high-stakes, or irreversible work with enough state for safe review and continuation.

nodes.label: Tool contract design
nodes.summary: Give each tool a distinct purpose, unambiguous name, precise description, and schema that makes correct selection likely.

nodes.label: Tool selection and tool_choice
nodes.summary: Match automatic, forced, disabled, and parallel tool policies to the actual ordering guarantee required.

nodes.label: MCP tools, resources, and transport
nodes.summary: Choose MCP primitives by whether the capability performs an action, exposes context, or defines reusable interaction material.

nodes.label: MCP error semantics
nodes.summary: Return actionable tool errors with explicit failure and retry semantics so the agent can recover locally or escalate.

nodes.label: Least-privilege tool scoping
nodes.summary: Expose only the capabilities an agent or workflow needs, with credentials and scopes bounded at the enforcement layer.

nodes.label: Hooks and tool guardrails
nodes.summary: Use PreToolUse for deterministic prevention and PostToolUse for validation, feedback, and repair after execution.

nodes.label: Built-in discovery and editing tools
nodes.summary: Use Glob to locate, Grep to search, Read to inspect, and Edit for precise changes while preserving a bounded working set.

nodes.label: CLAUDE.md memory hierarchy
nodes.summary: Place stable guidance at the narrowest useful user, project, or directory scope and understand how nested memory applies.

nodes.label: Settings and permissions precedence
nodes.summary: Resolve configuration by scope and enforce access through permission settings rather than relying on prompt requests.

nodes.label: Skills, rules, and reusable guidance
nodes.summary: Separate always-relevant conventions from path-scoped rules and on-demand procedural skills.

nodes.label: Codebase exploration workflow
nodes.summary: Discover incrementally, inspect before editing, and keep findings scoped to the current task.

nodes.label: Claude Code in CI/CD
nodes.summary: Run bounded headless workflows with non-interactive permissions, machine-readable outputs, and explicit failure behavior.

nodes.label: Plan, execute, and verify
nodes.summary: Use planning for uncertain multi-file work, direct execution for bounded work, and verification proportional to risk.

nodes.label: Configuration versus enforcement
nodes.summary: Distinguish advisory instructions from deterministic permission, hook, schema, and CI enforcement mechanisms.

nodes.label: Instruction specificity and criteria
nodes.summary: State the objective, constraints, decision criteria, and edge-case behavior explicitly enough to guide judgment.

nodes.label: Few-shot examples
nodes.summary: Demonstrate desired classifications, boundaries, and difficult cases when prose rules alone leave behavior ambiguous.

nodes.label: Structured outputs and JSON Schema
nodes.summary: Use constrained structured output to guarantee syntax, types, required fields, and machine-parseable shape.

nodes.label: Semantic validation and repair
nodes.summary: Validate business meaning beyond schema shape, then retry or repair with targeted error feedback.

nodes.label: Extraction boundaries and ambiguity
nodes.summary: Define evidence boundaries, nullable behavior, and escalation for ambiguous or unsupported values.

nodes.label: Evaluation and confidence calibration
nodes.summary: Measure failure categories on representative samples and map confidence or severity to explicit actions.

nodes.label: Iterative refinement
nodes.summary: Separate generation, critique, and targeted revision when one-pass quality is insufficient.

nodes.label: Conversation history and tool results
nodes.summary: Preserve assistant tool_use blocks and keyed tool_result blocks in accumulating history so later turns can reason from prior actions.

nodes.label: Session identity, resumption, and state
nodes.summary: Resume the correct named session to preserve task state while keeping unrelated users and cases isolated.

nodes.label: Context budgeting and relevance
nodes.summary: Control token growth by selecting, trimming, and ordering the information most relevant to the next decision.

nodes.label: Context isolation
nodes.summary: Use fresh or forked contexts to prevent stale, unrelated, or conflicting state from contaminating work.

nodes.label: Progressive summarization
nodes.summary: Compress long-running history into durable structured summaries while retaining decisions, open work, and evidence pointers.

nodes.label: Prompt caching
nodes.summary: Reuse stable prompt prefixes to reduce repeated processing cost and latency without changing what information the model receives.

nodes.label: Provenance and structured handoffs
nodes.summary: Carry claim-to-source mappings, timestamps, and confidence through summaries and agent boundaries.

edges.rationale: The loop is the execution core of agentic architecture.
Reliable completion is an architectural control-flow concern.
Decomposition is a primary coordinator responsibility.
Subagent boundaries determine orchestration behavior.
Topology encodes dependencies and coordination.
Routing strategy is an architectural choice.
Human control and recovery are architectural safety patterns.
Contracts define model-facing tool usability.
Selection policy governs when tools execute.
MCP primitives are core integration mechanisms.
Error contracts determine recovery behavior.
Tool exposure defines the capability boundary.
Hooks intercept and validate tool execution.
Built-in tools are the standard code-work capabilities.
Memory files are central Claude Code configuration.
Settings scopes determine effective configuration.
Reusable guidance is a Claude Code workflow mechanism.
Exploration is a foundational development workflow.
Headless automation is a distinct Claude Code workflow.
Workflow selection and verification are core operating decisions.
Claude Code separates advisory guidance from enforcement.
Clear criteria are the basis of prompt behavior.
Examples shape behavior at ambiguous boundaries.
Structured outputs create machine-readable contracts.
Semantic checks address correctness beyond syntax.
Extraction reliability depends on explicit evidence rules.
Evaluation measures whether prompting works.
Refinement is a prompt workflow for complex quality goals.
History is the immediate context state of an agent loop.
Sessions preserve state across invocations.
Budgeting controls context scale and relevance.
Isolation prevents context contamination.
Summarization controls long-session growth.
Caching optimizes repeated stable context.
Provenance must survive context transitions.
An agentic loop needs protocol-level completion conditions to avoid premature or runaway termination.
The next loop iteration can reason correctly only when prior calls and keyed results remain in history.
Selection policy cannot compensate for overlapping or ambiguous tool contracts.
tool_choice changes which actions an iteration may request and whether parallel calls are allowed.
Explicit tool failure and retry fields tell the loop whether to retry, repair arguments, or escalate.
The loop is appropriate when the next step depends on observations not available up front.
Dependencies exposed during decomposition determine whether work may run in parallel or must be sequenced.
Assignments must be self-contained because subagents do not inherit coordinator or sibling context.
Fresh contexts create specialization and contamination resistance, but require explicit handoffs.
Structured handoffs keep evidence attached to claims across isolated agents.
Delegation can isolate verbose work, while budgeting limits what returns to the coordinator.
Coverage evaluation can trigger targeted re-delegation rather than repeating all work.
Local recovery handles bounded failures; explicit escalation handles failures the agent should not resolve alone.
High-risk capabilities should be bounded and routed through approval or escalation points.
A pre-tool hook can block or request approval before an irreversible action executes.
Effective permission settings enforce which tools and paths Claude Code may access.
A learner must distinguish advisory instructions from settings that deterministically deny capability.
Hooks are chosen when a requirement must be intercepted or validated rather than merely requested in prose.
Memory, path rules, and skills place different kinds of reusable guidance at different scopes and activation times.
Always-loaded memory should remain concise because it consumes context on every applicable turn.
On-demand skills and path-scoped rules avoid loading unrelated guidance into every task.
Glob, Grep, Read, and Edit implement the incremental explore-before-change workflow.
Exploration should add only task-relevant files and findings to the working context.
Exploration reduces uncertainty before planning and execution; verification closes the workflow.
Machine-readable findings eliminate brittle prose parsing in automated pipelines.
CI requires non-interactive, enforceable permissions and explicit failure semantics.
Blocking thresholds should come from measured severity and false-positive behavior, not prompt confidence alone.
Criteria state the rule; examples clarify how it applies at difficult boundaries.
Positive, negative, null, and ambiguous examples demonstrate evidence boundaries.
Schema validation establishes syntactic correctness before domain meaning can be checked.
A schema can guarantee shape but cannot guarantee that extracted values are supported or correct.
Validation failures supply categorized observations for evaluating quality and setting thresholds.
Validation needs explicit rules for unsupported, ambiguous, and nullable fields.
Measured failure clusters identify which critique and revision passes are worth adding.
Tool descriptions are prompts whose purpose, arguments, and selection criteria must be explicit.
A structured output contract makes isolated subagent results predictable to the coordinator.
Tool errors repair execution failures, while semantic validation repairs well-formed but wrong outputs.
Resuming the correct session restores the conversation and tool evidence needed to continue.
Session identity must prevent one user, case, or task from inheriting another's state.
Structured summaries make the context budget sustainable by reducing long-session token growth while retaining decision-relevant state.
Compression must preserve source pointers and distinguish supported facts from synthesis.
Caching lowers repeated processing cost, while budgeting reduces the amount and relevance burden of context itself.
Caching does not shrink or improve context; it only reuses eligible stable prefixes.
Stable shared instructions are natural cache-prefix material when API request ordering permits it.
MCP resources can expose discoverable context on demand rather than embedding every item in the prompt.
Explicit terminal error categories give a human the reason, state, and next action needed for takeover.
Traceable claims enable evaluators to distinguish unsupported assertions from supported synthesis.
Verification may trigger a targeted revision cycle when execution does not meet the plan's criteria.
